title: Asymmetry-aided measurement-based quantum repeaters and distributed quantum computing with a decoder-free client
authors: Wooyeong Song, Sungyeon Kook, Wonhyuk Lee, IlKwon Sohn
abstract: Distributed quantum computation needs to move logical qubits across lossy optical links, yet this transmission layer is usually designed separately from the computation it serves. We treat the two together by recognizing that a measurement-based quantum repeater is a two-dimensional code foliated along the transmission axis, so that the dominant channel loss is concentrated on the transmitted sector while the locally measured qubits are largely spared. Matching a code's distance to this structural asymmetry, we show that a rectangular Bacon-Shor subsystem code transmits a logical qubit markedly more efficiently than transmission-unaware encodings. Over continental distances, its cost-optimal repeater density is about an order of magnitude lower than that of a recent $[[48,6,8]]$ benchmark at comparable transmission rate, and roughly half that of a symmetric code of equal size. Moreover, we extend the framework to a central-to-client round trip in which a code-level, distance-preserving code switch joins the transmission legs to the client's computation, and joint decoding of the heterogeneous syndrome record at the central node lets distributed quantum computation proceed with a decoder-free client.
summary: This paper develops an advanced theory for distributed quantum computing over lossy optical links by treating the repeater as an integrated part of the computation. It shows that using highly asymmetric Bacon-Shor quantum error correcting codes—whose structure matches the unequal loss rates of transmission versus local measurement—dramatically improves qubit transmission efficiency. This approach enables robust, long-distance quantum networking with a simplified client architecture.
main_problem: The research addresses the challenge of efficiently transmitting logical qubits across lossy optical links while integrating this transmission layer directly with the quantum computation.
main_result: By matching the structural asymmetry of a measurement-based repeater (where transmitted qubits suffer more loss than local ones) to an elongated Bacon-Shor subsystem code, significantly higher effective transmission rates are achieved compared to symmetric codes or unaware encodings.
method: The authors model the quantum repeater as a two-dimensional code foliated along the transmission axis and derive optimal code geometries by balancing logical failure probabilities across different error sectors.
model_or_system: The system uses photonic graph states and CSS codes, specifically comparing Surface Codes (SC) against Bacon-Shor (BS) subsystem codes. The core mechanism relies on exploiting structural asymmetry in the channel loss rates ($p_Z$ vs $p_X$).
key_observables: Logical qubit transmission efficiency ($\eta_{eff}$), logical failure probability ($P_L$), and required repeater density.
important_parameters: Channel erasure rates ($p_Z, p_X$), code distances $(d_Z, d_X)$, and the degree of structural asymmetry exploited by the code.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the optimal performance is achieved by designing codes whose structure mirrors the inherent physical asymmetry of the lossy transmission channel.
figures_summary: Figures compare logical success probability versus channel loss for SC vs. asymmetric BS codes, showing superior resilience for the latter; other figures detail cost-optimal repeater density and code switching protocols.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need to integrate repeaters with computation, deriving the optimal asymmetric code structure using heuristic conditions, demonstrating this advantage via rigorous error analysis (comparing SC vs. BS), and finally extending the framework to complex central-to-client round trips involving code switching.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete theoretical blueprint for next-generation quantum networks by optimizing QEC codes specifically for realistic, asymmetric channel noise profiles encountered in long-haul fiber optics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. The measurement-based repeater as a foliated code (stages I–III, left to right). (I) A repeater-state generator (RSG) prepares two 2D code layers, a local X layer and a transmitted Z layer, linked by qubitwise CZ bonds. (II) The incoming Z layer from the previous node is stitched to the local X layer by qubitwise CZ bonds. The enclosed two-layer block undergoes the controlled-Z and X measurement, teleporting the logical information onto the outgoing Z layer. (III) The outgoing Z layer is transmitted to the next node, while the measurement outcomes are forwarded as syndrome data over a classical channel. Dashed lines denote qubitwise CZ bonds. Ancilla qubits are omitted for clarity....

FIG. 2. Logical success probability of four equal-size (N = 81) codes versus channel loss (ηr = 0.9, one repeater), all decoded with the same maximum-likelihood foliated erasure decoder. The asymmetric Bacon–Shor code BS(27×3) sustains the highest Psucc across the whole loss range, whereas the same elongation improves the surface code only modestly (SC(9 × 9) →SC(27 × 3)). Matching the aspect ratio to the channel bias pays off for the gauge-rich subsystem code but not for the topological one. Each point is 2 × 104 Monte Carlo erasure samples. Error bars are ±1 standard error and are smaller than the markers (maximum SE ≈0.004).

FIG. 3. Performance of optimized repeater architectures. Four equal-pair codes are compared. These are the ∼48-qubit pair BS(7×7) (symmetric) and BS(15×3) (asymmetric), and the 81-qubit pair BS(9×9) (symmetric) and BS(27×3) (asymmetric). The center prepares the logical qubit in a transmission-optimized asymmetric Bacon–Shor code BS1(m × n) (dZ = m ≫dX = n) and transmits it to the client. The channel loss enters as the transmitted-sector erasure rate pZ [Eq. (1)]. The client injects the incoming state into a surface code SC(m × m) through the fault-tolerant switch of the previous section, runs the computation (Pauli rate pcomp), switches to a return code BS3(m′ × m), and transmits it back (pZ again).
